entry.title: setup emacs (with journaling) on your phone
entry.content:
Hover over a footnote to read it in-place

Install termux and emacs

You can grab termux from F-Droid or GitHub.

The first boot takes a while, Once its done, install emacs:

pkg update
pkg upgrade -y
pkg install -y emacs git ripgrep fd

We'll stick to the terminal build for this, not the separate GUI emacs android app for reasons1

Where the files lives

Emacs can write in two kinds of places on termux:

  • The termux home, for example ~/Documents/org/. It stays inside termux's directory, and other apps can't read it.

  • System storage, for example /storage/emulated/0/Documents/org/. Other apps can read it too. You need to run termux-setup-storage to get access to it

    termux-setup-storage

Its best to keep them in a shared directory if you want your files to be shared or synced2 between devices.

Porting your config over to your phone

Emacs reads its config from the termux home, either ~/.emacs.d/ or ~/.config/emacs/.3 It's easier to keep the same layout as your computer.

You can bring your own existing config, here are some ways:

  • git: git clone <url> ~/.config/emacs
  • ssh: scp -r config/ phone:~/.config/emacs, with sshd on the phone.4
  • adb: adb push config /sdcard/Download/, then cp -rv in termux.
  • USB-OTG: copy with the android file manager, then cp -rv in termux.

It's best to not copy the packages or cache folders. Let emacs install its packages on the phone.5

Android specific emacs tweaks

Know that you're in termux 

(defvar my/termux-p (or (getenv "TERMUX_VERSION")
                        (file-exists-p "/data/data/com.termux")))

The environment variable alone isnt enough as termux only sets it in shells started by it.6

Wrap the GUI-only parts

Fonts, transparency, margins, and image sizes only matter in a GUI. You can wrap them:

(unless my/termux-p
  (setq doom-font (font-spec :family "SF Mono" :size 14))
  (add-to-list 'default-frame-alist '(alpha-background . 85)))

If the journal is on shared storage, you'll also want to keep emacs litter out of it.7

(when my/termux-p
  (let ((auto (expand-file-name "auto-save/" user-emacs-directory))
        (backup (expand-file-name "backups/" user-emacs-directory)))
    (make-directory auto t)
    (make-directory backup t)
    (setq create-lockfiles nil
          backup-directory-alist `(("." . ,backup))
          auto-save-file-name-transforms `((".*" ,auto t)))))

Clipboard if you like it

Emacs can use the android clipboard through Termux:API.8

pkg install termux-api
(when (and my/termux-p (require 'xclip nil t))
  (xclip-mode 1))

You can point org-directory at the folder you picked in section 2, and doom users can drop it in ~/.config/doom/config.el.9

Pick a capture method

Your journal can be one or more org files. org-capture appends to one file. org-journal writes multiple files based on your config.

Here's a small setup for each

org-journal: one file per day

org-journal reads the date from the filename, so the format needs %Y, %m, and %d.10

(setq org-journal-dir "~/Documents/org/journal/"
      org-journal-file-format "%Y%m%d"
      org-journal-date-format "%A, %m/%d/%Y")

Doom's (org +journal) flag turns this on and gives you SPC n j j. Other configs usually bind org-journal-new-entry somewhere.

org-capture: one file 

(setq org-capture-templates
      `(("j" "Journal Entry" entry
         (file+olp+datetree ,(expand-file-name "Journal.org" org-directory))
         "* %<%H:%M>\n%?"
         :empty-lines 1
         :unnarrowed t)))

Newer org deprecates file+datetree, so this uses file+olp+datetree.11 Doom binds SPC X j for it.

Either way, C-c C-c files the entry, and C-c C-k throws it away. Closing the terminal does neither.12

One tap capture

And finally, a home screen shortcut that opens a capture in a new emacs frame.

Prep termux

Install Termux:Widget from the same source as termux. The widget runs scripts through termux, so termux must allow commands from other apps, and a warm daemon to reduce boot times.

echo "allow-external-apps=true" >> ~/.termux/termux.properties
termux-reload-settings
emacs --daemon

The shortcut script

Save this as ~/.shortcuts/Journal and make it executable. The filename becomes the label on the home screen.13

#!/data/data/com.termux/files/usr/bin/bash
export PREFIX=/data/data/com.termux/files/usr
export HOME=/data/data/com.termux/files/home
export PATH=$PREFIX/bin:/system/bin
export LD_LIBRARY_PATH=$PREFIX/lib
export TERM=xterm-256color

# start a daemon if the server is not up yet
emacsclient --eval t >/dev/null 2>&1 || emacs --daemon
for _ in $(seq 1 40); do
  emacsclient --eval t >/dev/null 2>&1 && break
  sleep 0.25
done

emacsclient -t --eval '(progn (setq my/capture-return-home t) (org-capture nil "j"))'

# a dead frame can leave the daemon stuck inside the capture
if ! timeout 5 emacsclient --eval '(condition-case nil
    (dolist (b (buffer-list))
      (when (string-prefix-p "CAPTURE-" (buffer-name b))
        (with-current-buffer b (org-capture-kill))))
    (error nil))' >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  pkill -x emacs
fi

am start -a android.intent.action.MAIN -c android.intent.category.HOME >/dev/null 2>&1

The script expects a small flag and a hook in your config, so the frame closes after the capture:14

(defvar my/capture-return-home nil)
(defun my/journal-capture-finish (&rest _)
  (when my/capture-return-home
    (setq my/capture-return-home nil)
    (delete-frame)))
(advice-add 'org-capture-finalize :after #'my/journal-capture-finish)
(advice-add 'org-capture-kill :after #'my/journal-capture-finish)

Add the widget

Long press the home screen, open the widget list, find Termux:Widget, and drag the shortcut to a free spot. Pick Journal. A tap opens today's entry.15

Footnotes

Other resources

Guides that cover similar teritory:

  • Bring your Emacs to Android - If you decide to get the android gui instead
  • Surprisingly, Emacs on Android is pretty good
  • Capturing an org-mode entry using speech to text - a very cool shortcut, but I prefer not to speak my Journal out loud when I'm out and about lol
  • Emacs and Org-Roam on Android with Termux extra keys - absolute ball knowledge, go here after setting up emacs on termux, I love his websites design too
  • Use Emacs in GUI mode on Android - tiny article on running emacs x11 version on termux
  • Emacs on Android, use with Termux - a cocktail of mixing android app and termux binaries
  • Setting up Doom Emacs in Termux
  • Emacs: keep journaling on the go - a completely different approach, html instead of emacs
  • Emacs with speechd-el on Termux - espeak for emacs, seems platform agnostic

More References:

  • GNU Emacs Android manual
  • Termux:Widget
  • Termux storage
  • org-capture manual
  • Why F-Droid, not Play Store
  • Syncthing-Android fork
  • OnyX, an Android Emacs config (archived)
  • Orgzly and organice if you want an app instead.
1

The GUI app is a different emacs. It has its own config directory, so termux config and packages don't carry over. Doom doesn't officially support it yet. It also can't use git, ripgrep, and other termux programs. The terminal one feels more at-home and is easier for things like shortcuts

2

Some options are Syncthing, git, Nextcloud, or a USB copy. If you sync, it's safer to change one copy at a time and have a versioning system in the sync tool.

3

If both ~/.emacs.d/ and ~/.config/emacs/ exist, emacs uses ~/.emacs.d/. Doom keeps its own files in ~/.config/emacs and your private config in ~/.config/doom.

4

If you'd like ssh, run pkg install openssh and then sshd in termux. It listens on port 8022, and you can connect via ssh -p 8022 <user>@<phone-ip>.

5

You only need the init files and config folders your setup uses, for example init.el, early-init.el, lisp/, and snippets/. It's best to skip .local/, elpa/, eln-cache/, and straight/, since they're machine specific. Doom users can just copy ~/.config/doom and run doom sync 😎

6

Termux only exports TERMUX_VERSION to the shells it starts. An emacs started over ssh, or by the widget may not see it. The data directory is a more reliable way

7

Syncthing treats lock files and autosaves as changes. They add noise and can cause conflicts. Keeping them inside user-emacs-directory means they wont reach the shared folder.

8

Termux:API is an app plus a package. Install both from the same source as termux. xclip.el has a termux backend, and doom's :os tty module loads it for you. For a non-doom config, install xclip from ELPA if not already

9

The line is (setq org-directory "/storage/emulated/0/Documents/org/") for shared storage, or ~/Documents/org/ for the termux home. Doom's private config is in ~/.config/doom/. In non-doom emacs, put it in init.el.

10

A daily journal needs %Y, %m, and %d in the filename. A weekly journal needs %G and %V or the date parts, a monthly one needs %Y and %m, and a yearly one only needs %Y. This is also why org-journal can't keep a single lifetime file.

11

file+olp+datetree is the current name for the old file+datetree. The path can be absolute or built from org-directory with expand-file-name. :unnarrowed keeps the whole file visible, so you can scroll back to earlier entries while you write.

12

Closing the session leaves the entry unsaved. C-c C-c writes it to the file. C-c C-k aborts, and org may put the text in the kill ring instead of the file. Neither is a save.

13

~/.shortcuts holds shortcuts that run in a terminal session. The file needs execute permission, so run chmod 700 ~/.shortcuts/Journal. The am start at the end needs "Display over other apps" for termux on android 10 and later, or the launcher can stay behind the terminal.

14

emacsclient -t opens a terminal frame. Finishing or aborting deletes that frame, so you land back on the launcher. If the frame dies first, the daemon can be stuck inside the capture and stop answering. The timeout clears the capture, or restarts emacs.

15

For org-journal, replace the org-capture call with org-journal-new-entry. Whatever you use, finish with C-c C-c. The back button and closing the session do not save.

entry.title: What the Pho, Rosh? #1
entry.content:
Earlier this year I went to Vietnam on vacation. Most days were nothing short of an adventure that I wanted documented, so I could come back and (hopefully) laugh at it. But I gotta admit, some days were so adventurous that on one of the days, I actually prayed like Kareena Kapoor from Jab We Met.

Right from the moment I landed I have either lost precious items, made rookie mistakes or quite simply paid a price for mistakes that weren’t even mine. Let’s start from the top.

We’re going to call this adventure series “What the Pho, Rosh!” because ‘when in Vietnam?’

When I landed in Hanoi, Vietnam, I thought my first mini-adventure was losing a precious piece of earring that I had bought from a beach trip and worn just once. I lost it during the plane ride from Bangalore to Hanoi, and almost ended up filling the Lost & Found complaint form with the airline till I saw the line at the Immigration. It was like I entered the Tirupathi of Vietnam. 👀

(Yes, in hindsight, it’s a bad idea to wear a piece of jewellery that is precious to you while all you plan to do is sleep in the flight. I know now.)

I was so wrong about it being a mini-adventure. So much had happened since, that I would probably just categorize losing that beautiful jewelry as an omen for all that was to come. 

My first real adventure hit me when I so confidently sat in Bus No. 90 that would take me from the airport to my Airbnb. I had a smug smile on my face as I thought to myself “I have read all the instructions! I am going to travel like a local…” 

“THIKET”

…the conductor interrupted my (bus of?) thought by waving what looked like a credit card machine in his hand. It was not. It was ticket issuing machine and that’s it. My Forex card was rejected the instant I took it out of my wallet. “Cash only” is what he wanted to say when he took out a stack of VND (Vietnamese đồng) and waved it at my face. “One minute” I said, lifting my index finger up in case he didn’t understand, and started searching my bag for my wallet. And then, my luggage and then, my carry on. Oh hell..

Yep - my wallet was missing.

But unsuspecting Rosh from that day did not know that. Because she had a 6-page checklist that she had meticulously made, used it to pack for her Vietnam trip which included her wallet. And every item inside the wallet had not only made it to the checklist but also had all been checked off, TWICE!!! Which meant her wallet had to be inside the suitcase OR her backpack OR her mini-backpack - the only pieces of baggage she carried.

So, I frantically began searching both of them when it yielded no result. My wallet, which had just enough VND for a bus ride and a meal, was missing.

I fortunately had my Forex card and some dollars in hand thanks to my mini-backpack. But I was over-confident and hadn’t gotten my money exchanged at the airport, because I knew from my “research” (read: reddit and a good friend’s advice) that USD is worth more in the Gold shops of Hanoi than at the Noi Bai Airport. This pettiness would cause me to endure two hours of silent embarrassment while sitting in the bus, as a kind Vietnamese stranger would offer to pay for my ticket and assure me that it’s okay. I knew it wasn’t okay, I knew I’d messed up. But I obviously couldn’t tell him that. I just thanked him profusely and began wondering what to do.

I did the second best thing I could. I called my mum.

(Guesses for what would have been the first best thing are accepted in the comments. Brownie points for guessing why I didn’t choose that.)

The minute she answered, without even pausing to respond to her chirpy “Good morning, dear! How’s Vietnam?”, I asked her in one breath (and quite sternly, in retrospect :/ ) “Ma, will you be going to my house today? I cannot find my wallet. I need you to check my house.” Instantly, the quiet panic reflected in my mum’s voice, too “Yenna da…” she trailed and whispered at the same time, which would have been an endearing way of saying “What the hell, Rosh?” if the whisper did not make it scarier and embarrassing than it already was.

I quickly interjected her and said “I have my passport and my forex. DO NOT WORRY….” with as much emphasis and emotion as I could place in those three words. “But my important ID cards and INR are inside my wallet. I cannot find it in my bag. Can you please look for it in the house? Please? I just need some peace of mind”. That seemed to calm her a bit “Oh okay, so you have the dollars? I will get it checked. Did you eat something, do you need me to send money to you?” she enquired caringly, in the typical, parental, “I need to ensure my child’s wellbeing” mode. I assured her that I was fine and getting to the Airbnb. But as soon as I hung up, I admitted the truth to myself. I was not okay and what I did wasn’t okay, either.

Even the kind stranger assured me stoically when he paid for my ticket, “It’s okay, it’s okay”. But none of it felt okay. So I just sat with that discomfort for the next hour and a half. 

When the bus conductor handed the ticket to me I tried to read what it said - “15,000 VND” it read, along with the name of the last station. I quickly tried to calculate what the equivalent in INR is - “52.22” Google said. “Okay, I would also do the same to someone in Bangalore if it cost just that much… I would, right?” 

My mind was racing. A part of me tried to attach a monetary value to that kindness, a part of it tried to trivialize the gesture simultaneously. Another part began thinking back to a time when I had done a good deed just like this to a stranger from outside the country. It was almost as if I was trying to find reasons to feel like I was a rightful recipient of this kindness. (Relatable?)

After what seemed like fifteen minutes of this anxious thought-loop, I heaved a big sigh. “It’s okay”, I told myself as I continued to look out of the window. “You will find your wallet” even though all of me would not believe these words of reassurance. I didn’t want my people thinking that I couldn’t “take care” of myself as a solo traveller in Vietnam. Sigh.

entry.title: Thailand and the Moon Village Association convene Korean, Japanese, Chinese, and Western space organizations for sustainable lunar operations
entry.content:
Thailand is the only country in the world which has active civil and scientific space programs and is also party to the US-led Artemis Accords as well as China-led ILRS frameworks for cooperative lunar exploration. Which is why the Moon Village Association’s 10th global lunar symposium piqued my interest since Thailand’s leading space organization, called Geo-Informatics and Space Technology Development Agency (GISTDA), co-hosted the event in Bangkok last week on October 26 & 27. The fact that both US and Chinese government officials were present made the space event one of the few in the world of its kind. And that lunar operators from South Korea and Japan were presenting too convinced me to attend the event and cover notable highlights here on my Moon Monday blog+newsletter.

Editorial disclaimer: I asked the Moon Village Association (MVA) to cover my logistical expenses of air and lodging only in return for me writing about the event on Moon Monday, which they agreed to. I did NOT ask MVA to sponsor the coverage itself. MVA or GISTDA have no say, and requested none, in what gets covered and how so. In fact, they are able to read this coverage at the same time as all of you do: that is, when it’s published, which ensures editorial integrity.

While the program topics spanned a wide range, the standouts were talks and panels discussing the existing and impending challenges of lunar traffic management, especially in orbit. Two leading ones among those deliberated on ‘coordination in lunar operations’ and ‘lessons from terrestrial space debris governance for sustainable lunar activities.’ The conversation on the overall theme thus encompassed multiple sessions.

Lunar orbital coordination today

To understand the context in which lunar operators and their organizations surfaced challenges and possible pathways, we first need to understand the specifics of the situation at Luna. Our Moon may be one of the largest satellites in the Solar System but its exploration in this decade and next is being largely concentrated in select regions. One of them is low lunar orbit, where mapping spacecraft from three countries have been concurrently flying from pole to pole between 50 to 150 kilometers above the Moon’s surface for over four years. These comprise the US’ Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO), India’s Chandrayaan 2 orbiter, and South Korea’s KPLO spacecraft. The Moon’s gravity being uneven means they have to operate in select orbital planes which maintains their mapping orbits and avoids crashing into the Moon. But that also means their orbits often overlap, increasing the likelihood of these orbiters running into each other at high velocities.

The situation compelled their three space agencies—NASA, ISRO, and KARI—to start coordinating and sharing precise trajectory information of the lunar satellites with each other. Each satellite operator has thereby conducted many diversion maneuvers to avoid uncomfortably close passes with one or the other craft. Moon-Jin Jeon, the KPLO operations lead who spoke virtually at the MVA & GISTDA event has previously presented on the topic at the Secure World Foundation’s Summit for Space Sustainability event in 2024. Jeon had described how the three agencies use NASA’s MADCAP software to predict and alert operators of potential close approaches between their orbiters, after which a decision is taken by either craft to divert.

In October 2021, ISRO commanded the Chandrayaan 2 orbiter to slightly change its orbit to avoid a three-kilometer-close approach to NASA’s LRO. Similarly, LRO postponed a maneuver in 2023 to avoid more such close conjunctions. An August 2023 blog post by ISRO, which was specifically on the importance of managing growing lunar traffic, mentioned the Chandrayaan 2 orbiter maneuvering to avoid close approaches to KPLO. In turn, KPLO too has performed multiple such maneuvers. Even in 2025, despite better predictions, improved trajectory sharing, and increased coordination between parties, the Chandrayaan 2 orbiter still had to perform two collision avoidance maneuvers with LRO on January 1 and July 24 respectively.

Such maneuvers necessary for safety of operations will only grow in number in the coming years as more reconnaissance orbiters become operational amid increasing Moon missions worldwide. Upcoming orbiters expected to also occupy low lunar orbit as soon as next year are China’s Chang’e 7 and US-based Firefly’s Ocula craft. Several more are expected to launch through the rest of this decade.

Flight C3 International

Moreover, at the MVA & GISTDA event, China shared many details of their upcoming “Cislunar Cubesat Constellation (C3)” of 34 satellites, being built with international participation—Thailand included. Zhongmin Wang, Director of China’s International Cooperation Center at the Deep Space Exploration Laboratory (DSEL), presented the C3 mission’s three developmental phases before launch in 2030, and its scientific & technological objectives of demonstrating collective measurements of the deep space environment and lunar surface. Wang noted that 15 international institutions are participating in C3 at the moment, and that there’s room for more until next year. I wanted to write a whole article on this complex and inspiring mission but instead I thought of getting you something better in the moment: the full set of Wang’s slides. I approached DSEL and asked permission to share the slides and information publicly on Moon Monday. They agreed. Attached here is the presented PDF.

C3 lunar constellation updates | Wang Zhongmin, DSEL, China
wang-zhongmin-c3-lunar-constellation-updates-dsel-china.pdf
5 MB

Zhongmin characterized C3 as the “largest space environmental detection constellation ever”, which other than lunar studies will detect and localize gamma ray bursts from energetic cosmic objects with high precision. The nerds among us would love not just the mission’s functions but its name C3 due to the term’s characteristic role in the rocket equation. C3 the mission will not be in low lunar orbit. Instead, its 34 satellites will be deployed in a 1:3 elliptical resonance orbit of about 9 days between the Earth and Moon. The perigee will be ~10,000 kilometers and the apogee ~360,000 kilometers. Each C3 satellite will fly past the Moon periodically but together they will have numerous passes to collectively map the lunar environment and surface resources like water ice.

Alarming events

While C3’s trajectory avoids crowding low lunar orbit, other reconnaissance missions will still use that space, including a litany of landers who will pass through it temporarily but dynamically. To cite a real event, in 2024 KPLO avoided a close approach to Japan’s SLIM spacecraft before the latter’s Moon landing. [That ISRO’s Chandrayaan 2 orbiter separately aided SLIM’s precision landing adds another interesting layer to this cooperation dynamic.] What alarmed everyone involved was that KPLO’s maneuvering decision for SLIM had to be evaluated and taken within a single day. During the MVA symposium, Jeon highlighted this event and thus the increasing risks of cascading accidental collisions within the tight orbital mapping spaces our Moon’s gravity allows. Based on KPLO’s operational experience, Jeon stressed on two key takeaways, requesting the following from all future Moon missions:

  • Share updated orbiter prediction and trajectory plans with fellow operators in advance.
  • “Establish communications channels before launch.”

While the existing coordination between KARI, NASA, and ISRO has averted both loss of spacecraft and major cuts in valuable observation time, establishing said coordination earlier in the decade wasn’t easy to begin with. Citing roadblocks, Jeon noted that KARI’s initial emails to ISRO about potential orbital conjunction warnings got erroneously blocked by ISRO’s system protections. KARI had to go through NASA, who forwarded said emails. In a more fast-paced situation like KPLO’s one-day-maneuver for SLIM, such unexpected coordination blockers can become lethal. SLIM is not the only example of a lander-orbiter coordination, as evident within ISRO’s summary of its space situational awareness report about events in 2025:

The required coordination for spaceflight safety was carried out for all operational [lunar] satellites. For CH2O [the Chandrayaan 2 orbiter], such coordination with Firefly Aerospace, Intuitive Machines, and ispace [landers] during their lunar orbiting phase was facilitated by NASA.

It’s important to note here though that unlike South Korea and the US, no ISRO official or engineer was present at the MVA & GISTDA event in Thailand, physically or virtually. It’s an oddity considering that ISRO and GISTDA are already active space partners. So we have less visibility on ISRO’s side of lunar coordination beyond intermittent official posts on the space agency’s website.

Building a new lunar order

Regardless, the current coordination process being more manual than automated is thus slow, and will not scale as lunar activity grows, as was also noted in another panel than Jeon’s by Antonio Stark, Senior Business Associate at ispace Japan and also MVA’s Global Network Coordinator. Relatedly, ispace Japan and US-based Argo Corp announced earlier this year that the duo aim to deploy at least five lunar navigation and communications satellites by 2030, with the first one aimed for launch in 2027. The fact that there is no globally accepted and adopted lunar time standard will also become concerning as satellites crowd the tight low lunar orbit.

Alejandro Sela, CEO and co-founder of JAOPS, which commercially operated Dymon’s YAOKI lunar rover last year onboard Intuitive Machines’ IM-2 spacecraft, noted in the panel with Stark that data sharing connections between commercial companies are weak. Sela then highlighted how many lunar and space missions have begun using the open source mission operations software Yamcs, the shared foundation of which allows for easier data sharing between operators should they choose to. “Valuable operational data being shared would make our ecosystem more powerful.” To Sela’s point, JAOPS has in fact made public all the raw telemetry, telecommands, and images from YAOKI’s mission, which includes data distribution through a partnership with the Lunar Ledger of the Open Lunar Foundation (a Moon Monday sponsor). Data sharing in this manner could be a rising tide for all given the treacherous nature of the lunar south pole.

Global level coordination usually demands legally binding agreements between states. However, Yu Takeuchi, Director of the Space Law Research Center at Keio University in Japan, cautioned against enforcing this approach. Takeuchi highlighted in the same panel as Jeon’s that common understanding among various actors for operations doesn’t necessarily require legally binding measures. Imposing the latter can in fact reduce adoption in Takeuchi’s view, as has been seen in space history. During his panel, Stark likened information sharing challenges for commercial companies as a version of the “prisoner’s dilemma” wherein if only a few companies share information but others don’t, it creates unfair advantages for the passive players. In fact, this is the exact kind of problem the Lunar Ledger of the Open Lunar Foundation (a Moon Monday sponsor) aims to solve in a bottom-up manner by being a mutually trusted third party facilitator.

SSTL UK, which is about to launch the Lunar Pathfinder orbiter next year onboard Firefly’s Blue Ghost 2 Moon mission, had presence at the MVA & GISTDA event through Alex Da Silva Curiel, who leads the company’s international business. Curiel remarked how when deciding norms for Earth orbit, we humans did not think far enough ahead, giving us the current congestion situation and cascading collision risks. Mega-constellations weren’t originally considered at all when shaping terrestrial space norms. With the Moon however, Curiel expressed, we have a chance to do fundamentally better by planning far enough into the future.

In essence, everyone agrees that coordination at the Moon is needed. In practice, people are unsure of exactly how to coordinate, precisely what [not] to share, and when so. Towards the end of the symposium, I was reminded of what was stated in a recorded speech during the inaugural sessions by Aarti Holla-Maini, Director of United Nations Office for Outer Space Affairs (UNOOSA):

How we address these [sustainability] challenges today will shape the future of lunar exploration for generations to come. We have an opportunity and a responsibility to ensure that progress in science & technology is matched by progress in international cooperation.

Setting inspiring precedence along those lines, Jeon shared during his panel that the KPLO team has planned a controlled lunar impact of the satellite towards the end of its mission, which will avoid sensitive hardware areas and natural regions of international interest. Jeon added that KARI will share KPLO’s collision details in advance with the international community.

Many thanks to Catalyx Space and Gurbir Singh for sponsoring Moon Monday. If you too appreciate my efforts to bring you this curated community resource on global lunar exploration for free, and without ads, kindly support my independent writing as it’s purely reader-funded. I don’t use AI to write a single word and cite everything.

Support Moon Monday 🌙

- Jatan on jatan.space 🚀

entry.title: (#2026-W44) ganne ka juice and halloween game nights
entry.content:
The start of the week continued in the same haze from the previous week. Having fun when the ear is fine and mildly panicking when it started ringing. But I continued my medication religiously. ¶

Sometime during the week, the tech park hosted a Halloween-based fair in the common area, with many different shops selling different things. I’ve learned I’m keen about handmade shiny things, cups/mugs with cool designs, and things with flowers on them. Not flowers themselves though, they make me sneeze. ¶

I also found a telephone car thing, that looked very similar to a toy my sister had when she was little. A telephone she would drag around and its eyes would move up and down as its wheels spun. The tiny car was eerily similar, and I promptly sent a picture to my sister. ¶

I also realized that I have had more ganne ka juice (sugarcane juice) in Bangalore than I’ve had anywhere else. I don’t even remember having it outside of Bangalore. My parents told me a lot about how they would eat sugarcane as kids, so maybe I’ll tell them about the juice. They’ll probably ask about the hygiene of the place that’s making it. ¶

Halloween approached as the month of October ended. I’ve not had a proper celebration of Halloween in my life, so it’s just a Western event that passes over my feeds once a year. But I’m starting to feel like I want to know more about it. ¶

entry.title: [Weeknotes] Week of Nov 1st, 2026: Collaboration, man era, flash cards with friends
entry.content:
Work

New product at work. What this means is

  1. New codebase to learn the intricacies of. We've ported a lot of the hard stuff over - our eval framework, our admin definitions and privileges, the way we do auth. But there's a new architecture here and I don't yet know what it is.
  2. New way of writing code. We rebuilt Claude Tag (we're calling it a software factory) and load balancing all the work across all our machines. This way the work and the prompting happens on slack - which means it is much easier for us to pull in each other when we want more detail.

This is an attempt to

  1. Circumvent the cycle of building something that is subtly different from what is good for the product
  2. Accept that the LLM is mostly good at what we want it to do if provided with very strong defaults and constraints (the constraints are built into the factory)
  3. Move the process of building from being very individualistic to being more collaborative.

LLMs have made it easier than ever for people to disappear down a rabbit hole, learn what they need to, and come up for breath with a strong opinion. As a young engineer, if I told baby Tanvi that my instinct would be to not ask a human questions and for collaboration, I would be appalled! But ngl, I really enjoy the process of understanding and building a new thing with an LLM. I am able to shed my ego and ask about the same thing from different angles, or find different points of relation, or work all the different angles so that I have a take and the understanding to back it up. This may also be a consultant tendency. I'm learning that when you work in an organization, it might be more valuable to go on this journey with your peers, as a more effective way to build consensus.

The new product is in the space of community-building - a space that is very dear to my heart. I am very excited to be more of a product thinker in this context. When I was younger, I wanted to be a product manager! But I'm really glad I stayed the path and acquired technical chops - I feel much more informed about executing my (or any) vision now.

I have at least 5 drafts that just need time to be polished and published (including those two eval explainers the way I use them) and several more in the outlines stage. I have allotted 2h a day this week to work on them. It's going to be intense but I am curious if I find it useful and keep the habit or tiresome and figure out a new thing. But one thing is clear - just like I now regularly allocate and spend weekend time thinking, I need to spend weekday time writing.

Life

This week has been very social! I went out for several meals, courtesy Restaurant Week

  1. Baan Phad Thai with a gang of 6, followed by coffee and excellent cake at Ondu Plate (happy birthday!)
  2. Boteco for a team lunch
  3. Mai Mai with Kenneth, Noopur, and Ankur for a mostly sushi and pork dinner
  4. Bistro Cameo for a sunny sunday lunch

We also had several people over, and I played entirely too many hours of Unrailed on the couch, classic co-op style.

I spent 5 shameful but glorious hours on dietsabya this week. Learnt about Komolika, whose style Lara Raj seems to have lifted as inspiration recently. I think - maybe - I would tentatively like to be on social media if the consumption is of culture curators like this (I am similarly partial to r/popheads) as opposed to meme content or comedy/influencer skits? I feel like there is more to think about and I feel better about it. Who are the current culture curators in our upper-class, english-speaking context lately?

Early in the week, I was still recovering from the sickness, and Devanjal and my aunt both insisted on feeding me, which I am very grateful for. Mum also came by and made me a tambali from the sambarballi growing in my balcony! Proud Plant Parent moment for sure (though my gardener and my help should take most of the credit for pruning and watering respectively).

I have not cooked for several weeks now. I am surprisingly happy and okay with this. A combination of people feeding me, frozen food from meal prepped large batches (that mom generously supplied!), and going out have kept me pretty happy and well fed. I have occasionally made eggs, maggi, or soup that would take less than 10 minutes (and less than 1 cycle of brain power). I am very happy to slowly morph into the straight raja beta I was meant to be. Being free of responsibilities - even for yourself and your house - frees up so much of the brain cycle time for thinking, doing, or recovering from all the thinking and doing.

Health

The flare continuous to flare. It is horrible. When will I be released from this mortal coil?? I have been exhausted. Today I took a general painkiller for the first time in I don't know how many months. Forget running, even walking 4k steps one day exhausted me so much I slept for ten hours that night.

A friend has recommended a new, different personal trainer who supposedly has a good track record and experience working with people with chronic illness. Do I trust them? In the last few years, I have been disillusioned by the fitness training world the way I was disillusioned by the medical field in my early twenties. Nothing can be outsourced. I have to do all the reading, research, collating, myself. I have to recognize the various interactions and contraindications, understand the implications, and make my own decisions. Some days I feel like I should get rid of this section entirely - thinking about this reminds me how nerfed I am. But I must remember. I must do something about this. Without my health I have nothing. I have fought so hard, and come so far, that regression is no longer a possibility. But I have plateaued - sacrificing the progress of better health for the ability to dive deeper at work.

I don't regret it yet? But I need to balance this now. I have a Very Large painscience.org article to read through (without getting distracted and following all the footnotes this time!). And i am getting back on gfdf. Let us hope the sacrifices please the inflammation gods.

Learning

Did my flash cards only three days of this week, but progress continues to be excellent. I spent an evening doing the flashcard recall with a friend who has also spent some time learning the kannada script. They had actually taken classes, so I learnt about how some letter forms are written in a way that is different from the font - there is not nearly as many twists and turns as print kannada makes it look like! I also found that reading handwritten kannada was much harder than reading the font. I am unsure where to practice this second skill from, apart from perhaps writing letters to my mother back and forth?

Things I need to spend time learning this week (there is urgency)

  1. The vagaries of various models that ai-sdk smooths out (and what it doesn't)
  2. How the router on our custom software factory works
  3. How to design a good benchmark for a model
  4. How steroids work, and what long-term usage does to a body
  5. Network reliability instrumentation

there really aren't enough hours in the day.

Media Diet

girl where is the time. I did visit the A Moving Line exhibit at MAP and added about 20 graphic novels to my to-read list, but I doubt a dent is being made in it any time soon. I would like to pick up India After Gandhi, and I would really like to read well-reported fashion ethnographies, but I don't think any exist in popular culture? I miss catching up on music videos as they come out. I have only been listening to singles, but they are all good. All the pop girlies are doing good.

entry.title: Baht-ing in your Thai-ness
entry.content:
Things I liked about Bangkok compared to Mumbai and Bangalore:

  • Vehicles follow traffic rules, slow down for pedestrians, and rarely honk. In Indian metro cities, honking is a language in itself.
  • The Thai city is clean.
  • People do not sit on reserved seats in metros, making it easier for the rightful people to use it.
  • You can hear silence in some places, an environment practically impossible to get in Indian metro cities.
  • The quality of fruits, even on random street stalls, is incredible.
  • Museums are fun and interactive.
  • Cigarettes are kept inside shelves in 7-Eleven shops with the blunt outer label “Harmful and addictive tobacco sold here.”

Things I did not like about Bangkok compared to Mumbai and Bangalore:

  • Many metro stations have no time indicators for the next train, and no escalators on some levels.
  • Payment methods are not unified across overhead and underground metros.
  • Cab apps are more unreliable, untimely, and expensive, even when normalized for purchasing power parity.
  • There are way too many malls. Consumerism in general thrives there.
  • Reading culture seemed very minimal; and I did explicitly seek events & groups. Mumbai and Bangalore really shine in this aspect.
  • Places with any good vegetarian food options are limited.
  • Access to public drinking water at restaurants or malls is rare.
  • Tuk Tuks literally ask for 100+ baht (₹300) for a single kilometer, paling even the brazenness of Bangalore auto drivers.
  • Local parks are not as prolific.
  • Plastic bags are given out for every single purchase, no matter how small.
  • It felt hotter than even Mumbai.

Other things of note in Bangkok:

  • There are so many massage parlors that one of them is literally called “One more massage”.
  • Some bathrooms in malls sell condoms LOL.
  • Traffic delays are as bad as any Indian city but the aforementioned driving traits make the roads more bearable.
  • People join hands and bow like in Indian culture to greet.
  • Thai Buddhism is infused with many non-Buddhist Indian cultural elements as well, specifically drawing from Hindu mythology and Brahmanism. Personally, I’m an atheist but I don’t mind drawing good behavioral ideas from any and every religion & culture.
  • Ramayana is famous here, adapted with Thainess. It’s so popular in fact that hand sanitizers are sold with Ramayana symbols and graphics on them. Cleanse your body and soul.
  • People in public spaces do not like to make eye contact at all. And they stand in lifts in opposite directions to another person.

Every single time I visit another country, I become conscious of some of the daily struggles of living in Indian cities. At the same time, I freshly realize the things that are actually better or cheaper here, which we don’t appreciate sometimes.

entry.title: lazy sunday bibimsaadam
entry.content:
woke up late today. well 9 am is late for me, as I typically end up waking up between 6:45 and 7:15 whether I want to or not.

breakfast was brik oven sourdough (really worth if available, stands up to loaves sold for 2-3x the cost of this) and avocado spread at about 10.

I have been tinkering with Septabee a music production DAW unlike any other software I have laid my hands on. It is incredibly optimized, makes absolutely no sense but can just be described as the product of genius. I'm not really a musician but I love messing with music production. It's so satisfying to me to stack a bunch of waves, effects, filters and patterns to create things that sound interesting.

I couldn't quite muster up energy to do something elaborate and did not have enough appetite to order in. Wanted to make something simple but tasty, but not what we had been eating all week.

Bibimbap is a korean mixed rice dish (bibim = mix, bap = rice) that features crispy rice toasted on a hot stone pot, fresh vegetables and a very moreish and slightly spicy sauce. Here's my take on it, I call it bibimsaadam, a mix between typical tamil style "variety rice" and bibimbap.

decided to share my take on it as a 15 minute dish, built for lazy november sundays

serves 2 vegan, vegetarian, dairy-free (but you can remix and adapt to whatever you want to add)

Ingredients

  • 1 cup rice
  • vegetables (what i used, change as you please)
    • 1 cup grated carrot
    • 1 cup chopped spinach (palak)
    • 1 cup chopped mushrooms
  • spices
    • some kind of warm spice mix like garam masala - i used 1 tsp of a mysterious blend left at home by my mother-in-law
    • umami-rich spicy sauce - i used Lee Kum Kee's black bean sauce but would also suggest an XO sauce, any lao gan ma, gochujang or pixian chili bean paste. hot sauces could also work, but they typically plenty of vinegar which I don't think works well in this dish.
    • salting agent - table salt works, but i used maggi sauce (picture below for the unenlightened few).

Preparation

  • pressure cook rice with the dry spice mix in a cooker for 10 minutes (or cook in a rice cooker which might take twice as long)
  • while that's cooking, toast the vegetables and mushrooms in very little oil for a few minutes until soft
  • add the seasoning sauces and salt and mix well
  • add the cooked rice, mix well and increase the heat
  • alllow the rice to get nice and toasty, you don't need to risk burning it in the pursuit of perfect nurungji but doing this even a bit gives the rice some chew
  • plate and eat while hot, as simple as that

ate this while starting a rewatch of fullmetal alchemist: brotherhood. Gosh this show was well made. overall 10/10 weekend.

entry.title: Spooky Mushroom Parottacos
entry.content:
Yesterday, Kat invited us and other friends over for a halloween x birthday hang with pumpkin carving, snacks, homemade mulled wine and apple cider and plenty of wholesome banter.

We decided to make something easy to grab and eat without a plate, flavourmaxx yet still be vegan friendly and not too spicy

Serves 4-8 vegan, vegetarian, dairy-free

Ingredients

  • 8 small malabar parottas, we used ID brand
  • 2 tomatoes, chopped
  • 2 onions, chopped
  • 7-8 garlic cloves, diced
  • 500 gm button mushrooms, each mushroom cut into 4 quarters
  • spice mix (can just use store bought fish fry masala paste, which is actually vegan)
    • 2 tsp chilli powder
    • 1 tsp turmeric powder
    • 1 tsp salt
    • 1/2 tsp garam masala
    • 1 tsp coriander seeds
    • 1.5 tsp tamarind
    • 2 tsp cumin
  • 1 tbsp oil (we use mustard, but its divisive - can use neutral vegetable oil as well)
  • avocado spread
    • 1 overripe avocado, mashed until paste
    • salt, lemon juice to taste

Preparation

Spice Mix

  • roast coriander seeds, cumin, and tamarind piece in a pan until raw smells disappears
  • add oil and dry spices, continue to roast without allowing it to burn

extra arsam funk: use mustard oil and sichuan peppercorns to make this slap harder

  • blend in a grinder to a paste

Mushroom Masala

  • Use a thick bottom pan, well seasoned cast iron or non-stick. this dish has the tendency to clump since we're going to be aggressively reducing water content
  • Heat oil, add garlic and fry
  • Add onions
  • Add tomatoes
  • Add spice paste and mushrooms, mix well
  • Keep it cooking for about 15 minutes, the mushrooms will start releasing water and the dish will become a thick jammy consistency
  • Continue reducing until majority of the water disappears and it starts sticking to the pan, stir constantly to avoid burning, stop the heat when reduced. taste and adjust salt

Assembly

  • cook the parottas more on one side than the other, with neutral oil - one side is to be fully one, the other side half done.
  • spread the avocado crema on one half of the fully cooked side of the parotta (we are going to be folding it over)
  • add a generous ladle of mushroom masala over the avo crema over same half of the parotta
  • fold the parotta over the masala and gently press; should look like a quesadilla or taco
  • toast again to cook the outside, gently flipping.

2026-10-31 22:51:24 s: If we go deeper into it, there’s two modalities to consider from a sociological perspective: that of individual developer towards the fringes of the social graph, connecting none or few edges to them, and the ones closer to the centre.

At the beginning, some may contribute with bug reports and small patches as fixes to them, building rapport as they become more prolific, prominent, across multiple projects, till they become core developers of such projects. Their path of gradual development is getting cut off or severely hindered from competition with LLM generated code. (The same situation, or worse, inside a company, especially when dealing with code that wont cause severe damage should things go wrong.) If you consider what Terrence

Tao had to say with regard to the way mathematics usually develops and how that is being affected (I say threatened) with the use of LLMs, we can borrow and adapt it to apply in our case: in the manner of building rapport, building a relationship of guidance, of mentorship by senior developers to junior ones, that ensures the inheritance of the wealth of invaluable experience, of tacit knowledge, to following generations; how does LLMs disrupt this process and what will be its repercussions should this process be hindered in this manner?

For example: Rich Hickey (Clojure), Andrew Kelly (Zig), perhaps Drew DeVault (SourceHut) to name a few. ((The process of delegitimization of the spiritual leadership of RMS in free software movement is another matter entirely, regarding the delicacy with which we needed to seperate his views regarding software freedom and his other views that caused him denouncement.)) When decisions of few affect a large number of people, arises politics naturally. Then there’s forking of software due to disagreement with how software is to be developed (the forks of BSD, MariaDB, Forgego, Vinyl Cache, Fossify, perhaps we can count Libera.chat as well?). Apart from benevolent dictatorship, there could be democracies like Debian and Codeberg e.V. as well.

On the other hand, there are leaders like DHH who brought mainstream politics directly into the domain of discourse within the FOSS community, such that no one needed any longer to hide behind the fig leaf of purported ‘apolitical’ nature of software. Again, codes of conduct present in various repositories are expression of, and commitment to, respect towards, and intent to uphold, within their modest means, human dignity and values, from respective communities in their limited shared space. Work towards those new programmers who inadvertently find themselves in the wrong side of the aisle, out of rebelliousness than of actual malice, to have them realize they’ve been associating with the wrong kind of people and rehabilitate them, at least those who didn’t go into the deep end and turn irredeemable, ‘saving’ whomever as much as possible. Compare similar effort w.r.t. inceldom.

After writing out this, do I realize how much have I observed over time, even as mostly an outsider.

2026-10-31 22:57:44 s: Sorry (but not really) for dumping half a blogpost worth of text. Enjoy :D

2026-11-01 08:43:00 s: Continuing from where I left and got a bit sidetracked, the derivation of meaning, was it.. again a spectrum between these two extremes: one of reverence of the spirit of computing, programming, and one of regard as a tool, a mere means of livelihood, people distributed in between, perhaps even moving in certain direction.

Reverence of the spirit manifests through a certain kind of sanctification of the process and the resulting code; I don’t mean in a strictly religious sense, please generalize to see what I’m intending to convey. In practice, we are talking about ensuring quality, correctness, performance, security and so on. These are all desirable in code, and developers may feel an intrinsic sense of validation, satisfaction, in being able to uphold their role of sincerity, through the extent to which they can realize these in their code. There’s also extrinsic validation from peers through performance of such realization, in the manner of profilicity. (See research by Moeller and D’Ambrosio on sincerity, authenticity and profilicity as ‘identity technologies’.) We can see the ‘worship’ (again generalize, or find me better analogies to describe the collective motivational framework and organization as such) of the former in myriad books, research articles, blog posts that expound on their importance, develop ways to better achieve them and so on. When the latter, external validation, which by no means less important in regards to the development of self-esteem, yet can still go awry is perhaps demonstrated through the example of the overzealousness with Rust. This is where a little of the ills of religiosity manifests overtly: in the proliferation of ‘rewrite in Rust’ movement or outright blame and shame of developers that has happened from not adopting Rust (at all or well enough) in many existing projects. On one hand there’s extensive research behind affine typing, borrow checking that allows Rust to provide the gurantees of memory safety, yet it’s not a panacea of other ills of software, that is to say, this zeal is perhaps unbalanced with regard to benefits obtained vs amount of effort need to be put in. Not all software is as mission critical to need rewrite into Rust, they can still manage with existing automatic memory management systems. More research on finding better developer experience of ensuring memory safety need to be carried out as well. I heard similar stories for X11 to Wayland transition. Matters behind systemd and init systems are something else entirely; that’s for another day to discuss in depth.

The matter of mere means of livelihood is perhaps better understood when generalized to motivation behind studying, acquisition of knowledge in the first place. Some study because they genuinely like it (count me in here), from purely intrinsic motivation, some others have extrinsic ones. The latter can be laid down in a spectrum: from personal gain to bringing benefits to society and humanity overall. The manner of selfishness is exemplifed in seeking lucrative jobs and limiting coding strictly as a means of obtaining better livelihood, to ensure upward social mobility, disregarding ethics involved in code, perhaps not gaining any intrinsic reward from authorship of code, or not taking it seriously. See earlier discussion about rehabilitation (let’s call it ‘conversion’, or to reappropriate a word: ‘jihad’, quite apt for the struggle involved, from the misuse in Indian media; also see ‘Butlerian jihad’ for comparison.)

Most relevant to us, is the betterment of society and perhaps humanity as a whole. Meaning here is primarily obtained from the users of software who benefit from it and express their gratitude. There’s a nuance involved, in that there need to be the development of a healthy relationship between the developers and users. It wont be good in the long term should the developers get burned out delivering value, yet continuing to get disparaged/disrespected from users with a sense of entitlement, for more features and so on. (Similarly for security, see xz incident. Similarly LLM generated pull requests, especially ones without demonstration of understanding of the code, as exemplar of disrespect/disregard to the time and effort of the developer.) A sense of mutual respect, recognition need to be fostered. As such, those disgruntled users of existing proprietary software gets introduced to free software, that they receive a modicum of understanding about the values involved in organizing and maintaining the movement. To put it succinctly, muft nehi, mukt. It helps us that we can rely on the rich philosophical tradition associated with the concept of mukti. Quite relevant in the Indian context, where people are eager to get a bargain, ignoring and disregarding what cost might be behind, that we make it clear at the first instance, before they get the wrong idea and any misunderstanding can form. I’d recommend reading through this rather dense post (as well as other writing you can find there) regarding ideas that are relevant to us, appropriately generalized:

https://coding.social/blog/reimagine-social/#social-coding-commons

2026-11-01 09:40:49 Akshay S Dinesh: The last part on the relationship between developers and users is where I think prav reversed it fully and got to the other extreme. As in, usually there’s a balance between users and developers in free software where users sometimes contribute and developers in general take user feedback into consideration. Because of the friction between Daniel and others, Prav decided to go full on “let’s ignore developers and build something fully user centric”. In that process, I believe, it has become unsustainable (prav people here may disagree)

entry.title: What's in a Name
entry.content:
There was a recent prompt in the IndieWebClub in Bangalore. What’s the story behind your domain name? I thought this would be a good way to talk about what the name skaup means, and what all other names this (and I) could have had.

My name is Saachi Kaup and I'm really glad to meet ya. This domain name is ofcourse skaup (pronounced: Es Cop). But why that and not others?

Let us rule out some others. Why not saachi-kaup as a username? Well mostly because this shows who I want to be more than I really am. So the name is gender neutral because I grew up quite tomboyish and like to carry that spirit over. And I would prefer to let people figure out I am a woman by reading these. It's delaying the inevitable, but that is our business in life anyways.

Well what next - yes what is up with my surname then. Who prefers their strange surname to their weirdly normal name? Well so backstory time. My parents grew up in Mumbai. But my family is from the southern part of India - Karnataka. Our native language is Tulu, a local language spoken in the coastal regions mainly. And in Tulu, the surname "Kaup" actually means nothing. "Kapu" is a coastal village in Karnataka. This next part is completely anecdotal. In my head, Indian surnames fall into a few categories - your caste (classic), your dad's name, your native village (like your's truly), some initials, or your family's historic occupation (Parsi people with their surnames like "doctor-wala").

Again these can mix and match. You can have your dad's initials as your surname, or your native village's initials. But you must have observed it's mostly "Dad's" here. Well, some south Indian families (like mine) have a matrilineal structure. AKA the property goes to daughters in the family and their children. So strictly speaky my surname should not even be "Kapu". It should be "Suvarna". My grandmother's maiden surname. Which she changed after marrying. The only reason she changed it was because coming to a more northern part of the country means assimilating. Put a pin on it.

But that still doesn't explain why a village named "Kapu" becomes a surname "Kaup"?

This is what I remember being told. When our ancestors moved from the village of Karnataka to Mumbai in search of a better life, we realised something. The sound of "Kapu" is embarrassing. In Hindi, the language spoken in Mumbai primarily (Can of worms to remain closed for now), there are a lot of words and phrases that effectively amount to something silly if they end with the u sound. For example chomu, buddhu and bhondu in hindi respectively mean stupid, stupid and stupid. Colloquially, if you want to make fun of someone, even lightheartedly, you just pick one of their attributes and add a u to it. Lambu is tall guy, chotu is short or young guy. And other things I won't say to keep it semi professional.

So all this was to fit in. In fact I even sat next to north Indian classmates in school."Kaur", "Kaul" etc are common north Indian surnames. A strange loop of assimilation.

The assimilation did not stop with the elders but. When some school kids would say "Call the Cops!", I'd be able to laugh it off. Haha, real original guys. Try picking a non uncle insult. But not if they said they were travelling to coastal Karnataka. If someone figured that out, it would be the end. "Saachi Kapu" - What a mess. Later on, there were kids who went to a Manipal, a famous college near Kapu beach. They would come back and say hey your surname, it sounds kind of familiar. And I would say to them "SHH, keep your mouth shut".

All this changed when I went to Kapu beach. It's a clean and beautiful beach. Coming from Mumbai atleast, it is a sight. Wow, these things can be clean? The lighthouse overlooks the beach stretch. There are a few rocks. They looked like hills to me when I was younger. And if you manage not to get vertigo, you'd see where the uphill green trees meet the sand and water. It's something else. So with hindsight, all of the earlier nonsense is just funny. I'd just say to them, does your native place have a lighthouse? Then shut your mouth.

Photo Courtesy of Sai Chintala's Blog

Or so I thought. I have been using it as a fun little ice breaker for years. But turns out on digging a little more, this entire story is made up. Stupid, stupid and stupid. Nobody was ever embarrassed of "Kapu". The BRITISH came in and changed the name of the Post Office from "Kapu" to "Kaap". And then this game of Chinese whisper began.

So now there are two things that happened. Either kid me, out of embarrassment, made up this story, or the adults around me, in order to get me to shut up, made up this story. Will choose the latter explanation to protect myself.

So, what does "Kapu" mean? Well there is a lot of history of the place. Tipu sultan ruled, then the British. They put up the lighthouse. The word Kapu in Tulu means to wait or to guard. Waiting I am certainly not good at, but guarding is not so bad. Regardless, it is my name. And you can do a lot of things with your name. You can change it. Christine to Ladybird, Archibald Leach to Cary Grant, Srivastava to Bachchan. Or you can twist and turn it around like I did. You can choose to be embarrassed. But it's nicer to think of lighthouses.

  1. Mariamma Temple in the village

  2. Kapu Wiki

  3. Againm, Photo Courtesy of Sai Chintala's Blog_

Post Notes

entry.title: Antipatterns in Gentrified Thindi
entry.content:
As someone who grew up in this city, I saw the South Indian Breakfast joints or darshinis go through a huge change in perception. They always had their cultish fanbases, but to a vast number of Bangalore's immigrant populations, they were often seen as unattractive.

But the food was always cheap, fast and really really good. Dose and medhu vade dippu eaten in a stand-up darshini is an integral part of my childhood.

To me, these places had a huge change in perception ever since the enterprising folks of Rameshwaram Cafe opened their joint in Indiranagar 12th Main, which was basically the same idea, but provided a more expensive Tamil-Kannadiga frankenthindi, and with a lot more flash and a lot more ghee. It almost seemed like the place was intentionally designed to form a large crowd that used to block the street, which fed into a certain kind of hype. Then influencers latched on to it, and brought Darshinis kicking and roaring into a gentrified modern form.

Surprisingly, I don't mind these places as long as they are not displacing the classical thindi spots1. It's good to make this cultural success more legible to people who otherwise were not going to give it a real shot. However, there are certain things that I find distasteful about them. If you are going to depart from the formula, the innovations need to actually be good. If you are starting a "gentrified" thindi joint, consider not doing these to stand out, and I will praise you.

Here are some antipatterns (in my opinion):

  • Drenching everything in too much ghee. It's often done as some weird display of flash and "purity" (often involving a cut in corner of a Nandhini packet and launching a urinary trajectory into the Dose or Idly). I like ghee, and the dopamine hit feels good for the first couple of bites, but it's too heavy to enjoy after that and I feel like I need to take a shower after I'm done eating.

  • Temple aesthetics and motifs. I'm bored of the flower patterns, grey stones, black plates with a vestigial banana leaf on top, peacocks and the likes.

  • Flavoured coffee. The filter coffee does not need hazelnut syrup, vanilla, or other synthetic flavours mixed into it that taste terrible. There are better variables to play with here: Indian spices, chicory percentages, roast levels, alternative milk, etc.

  1. My anecdotal observation is that they are often not displaced—a Rameshwaram or Filter Coffee in Indiranagar is most likely going to displace some lousy cafe or bar, and these gentrified places won't survive the competition in a Basavangudi or Cubbonpete. ↩

entry.title: tension
entry.content:
Tension is good, mostly. It is the pull that gives meaning to all art, and thus to life itself.

Anyone who is never tense about anything ever, has no payoff to look forward to.

Even the most easy-going happy movie, will employ various forms of tension-building to make the movie entertaining. Tension can be as blatant as introducing a problem that a character has to solve, or as subtle as giving the viewer the sense of, "Where is this going? What is going to happen next?"

A good DJ is a master of managing the tension of the crowds. Have a crescendo too often, and the payoff is not satisfying. Hold the tension for too long, and you lose the crowd.

Where tension fails is when it is building with no payoff in sight. Or if the payoff is fake, a total mirage, but you delude yourself into thinking there is a payoff.

Tension can be played with in hundreds of ways, and a big part of creativity is taking this strange polymer and moulding it into various forms. Sometimes you can stretch tension for so long that you lose the crowd, but then gain it back. Sometimes there's a payoff from the fact that there's no payoff, and that's the payoff. Sometimes you refuse to let tension build and release it so often that the repeated pattern of doing so becomes a new overarching pattern of tension building.

Sometimes, tension can be built with repetition of the word tension.

The whole is never just a sum of the parts. There are lots of things that I find to be disgraceful only when taken in aggregate. But any individual instance of it seems okay, and so I look odd when I object to any of these things.
